bio.en: Andrew Ambrosino is the product and engineering lead for the Codex app at OpenAI, which is quickly becoming a go-to tool for building products with AI.
bio.zh: Andrew Ambrosino 是 OpenAI Codex 应用的产品与工程负责人，该应用正迅速成为用 AI 构建产品的首选工具。

summary.en: Andrew notes that 90% of OpenAI's entire company uses Codex and aims to make it the best desktop app ever, with quality high enough that it becomes people's natural default. He argues design remains hard for frontier models to grade because taste is inherently human, and that implementation is no longer the expensive part—taste is. The conversation covers how product teams are shifting toward everyone being agentic builders and the risks of prematurely eliminating the PM role.
summary.zh: Andrew 提到 OpenAI 全公司 90% 的人都在使用 Codex，并致力于把它打造成史上最好的桌面应用，质量之高让它成为人们的自然默认选择。他认为设计对前沿模型而言仍难评判，因为品味本质上是人类的，且实现已不再是昂贵环节——品味才是。对话涵盖产品团队正向“人人都是能动型构建者”转变，以及过早取消 PM 角色的风险。

(00:04:20): And so what you want to do is you want to de-risk all implementation upfront through documents, through research, through prototypes. turns.zh: 现在作为 leader 建这些产品最难的事之一就是过程中的 inversion 在我脑里，很多人谈过，就是任何人能 build 任何东西。我 general 相信现在从零开始、如果你和这些模型聊、我们的、任何别人的，你能 stand up 你要的任何 feature。那不一定是软件难的部分，但很酷。(00:03:44)：我觉得那创造了环境大家在 build 一切。你给人无限 token。OpenAI 每个人非常 agentic、有好 idea。所以每个人在 build 一切。而我觉得你回头看我们跑了很久的产品流程它有点相反。是 research、ideation、也许一些 prototype。但即使过了 waterfall 它仍有点 flavored 实现贵。(00:04:20)：所以你要做的是通过文档、research、prototype 提前去 risk 所有实现。因为 prototype 和设计更便宜是那里的假设。那个变了。完全变了。(00:04:35)：现在我确定有 90 个不同探索 for……有个 feature 我们急需做、我确定有 90 个不同 uncoordinated 团队在实现和试，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.

What should we fold into other aspects of this? How should we frame this? Should it be part of this other feature? How many segments should be in the toggle? All of those things.
turns.zh: 所以短答案是它反过来了。不是说人在做根本不同角色或聚焦不同事或甚至 skillset 消失或角色消失。是它反过来了。实现其实不再是贵部分。是，我敢说，品味。(00:05:07)：但它是 curation 过程。像那 90 个尝试中这些有什么好？该 fold 进别的什么方面？该怎么 frame？该不该是别的 feature 一部分？toggle 该几段？所有那些。

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah. There's a lot of this. And it's not just happening here. You've seen many product leaders say PRDs are dead and prototypes are in. And I actually don't believe this at all. (00:07:17): I think that one of the interesting things that is happening right now is that because implementation has gotten so cheap across every medium, it's very tempting to jump straight to a prototype. Let me just show you what I mean." (00:07:45): What I've also noticed though is that for engineers, it's really tempting to write a lot of documents, a lot of documents that are not worth reading. This is no shade on people writing documents. It's that if implementation is abundant, then it's really important to pick the right format for the point you're trying to make. (00:08:05): If that point is product clarity around a vague area, then it might actually be a document. If what you're trying to do is get something in people's hands to try out and to stress test an interaction pattern, it's a prototype. But I think this is kind of the funny thing now, which is that it's really important to pick the medium.
turns.zh: 对。有很多这个。不只这里发生。你看到很多产品 leader 说 PRD 死了、prototype 在。我其实完全不信这个。(00:07:17)：我觉得现在发生的有趣事之一是因为实现跨每个 medium 变那么便宜，很诱人直接跳 prototype。尤其如果你不是工程师。尤其如果你从没能写代码或从没兴趣或从没时间，很诱人说 PRD 死了让我 show 你我什么意思。(00:07:45)：我也注意到对于工程师很诱人写大量文档、很多不值得读的文档。这不是 shade 写文档的人。是如果实现丰富那就很重要为你试图说的点选对 format。(00:08:05)：如果那个点是关于模糊领域的产品清晰度那其实可能文档。如果你要做的是给人试、stress test interaction pattern 那 prototype。但我觉得这个 funny 的是选 medium 很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this term that a podcast guest shared that I think about when you say this, which is it's called the primal mark. When a designer or a painter or an artist just creates the first mark on a painting or a piece of art, that mark is what you start to respond to. And so everything kind of trickles down from that first mark you make. (00:08:47): And what I'm hearing you saying is sometimes the prototype is the wrong first thing to do because then you're just responding to this prototype versus a different idea versus a bigger idea. turns.zh: 有个播客嘉宾分享的术语我说这个时想到的，叫 primal mark。当设计师或画家或艺术家在画或艺术品上 create 第一笔，那个 mark 是你开始回应的。一切从那个第一笔 trickles。(00:08:47)：我听到你说的是有时 prototype 是错误的第一件事因为然后你就回应这个 prototype vs 不同 idea vs 更大 idea。我爱听这个。大家就 okay 忘了不再写、不再 doc、不再 PRD。你说它们其实仍对特定用例有用。

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah. I think too, there's this part of the previous world was that the medium implied it had baked in a lot of signal around where in the process something was. So if you're seeing something that feels like the app in production, that means that it's late in the process. That assumptions have been de-risked, that design has looked at this, that this is a good business goal. (00:09:32): And now those things are sort of divorced. And the reason it was that way is because it was hard to get resources to build the thing until it was properly de-risked. And now that's just out the window. And so I think it's really important to start saying, "Look, we can have prototypes. We can have documents. Are we clear around what this is doing?" (00:09:51): Because to your point, you do not want to over anchor on this thing that was meant to be an exploration, but now it looks so production ready that, oh, visually it's ready for prod. But it's not actually the right model of where the research is going or what users are asking for or what's right for the business. (00:10:08): Not to overdo the taste thing, but it's once again, it's like the taste to know what to work on, how to present that information, how to achieve the goals, what medium to use is emerging as the most important thing to do. And that's in every field.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得 too 之前世界一部分是 medium implied 它 bake 了很多 signal 关于东西在过程中哪。如果你看到感觉像生产中 app 那意味着晚在过程中。假设已 de-risk、设计看过、这是好业务目标。(00:09:32)：现在那些 divorced。原因是以前很难得到资源建东西直到 properly de-risked。现在那个 out the window。所以很重要开始说说看，我们能 prototype、能 doc。我们清楚这个在做什么吗？(00:09:51)：因为如你所说你不想 over anchor 在这个 meant 是探索的东西上但现在看起来那么 production ready 以至于哦视觉上 ready for prod。但其实不是 research 在哪或用户在要什么或对业务对的 model。(00:10:08)：不 overdo 品味事，但再次就像知道 work 什么、怎么 present 那信息、怎么达成目标、用什么 medium 正在成为最重要的事。那在每个领域。

turns.zh: 你谈好品味时品味是什么？是你描述的决定这是我们要 invest 的？也是一旦有东西这是对吗？这是该 shift 的？(00:10:37)：聊你觉得好品味、好判断是什么具体？因为大家听这个词就哦我有好品味我知道。实际长什么样？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah. It's funny. There was a tweet, I'm too online. There was a tweet, I think it was yesterday from the head of product at Linear, I might be getting that wrong, sorry to anybody, who said, "People overemphasize the aesthetic part of what taste means." And they used, Paul Graham's great, but they used him as an example. Saying, "Paul Graham clearly has great taste and wears cargo shorts." (00:11:11): We got to tease out what taste means a little bit and there's a lot of nuance here. I think it's all of the above to what you mentioned. There is an aesthetic part to it, but there's also a systems thinking part of it, like how does this fit in the system? There's a where are we going and what theme is this part of? There's how to present this. (00:11:35): A lot of it is wider context. turns.zh: 对。有趣。有个推我太 online。昨天 Linear 产品负责人发的好像，我可能搞错对不起大家，说大家 overemphasize 品味的审美部分。他们用 Paul Graham great 但用他做例子。说 Paul Graham 显然有好品味、穿 cargo shorts。(00:11:11)：我们得 tease out 品味什么意思、很多 nuance。我觉得你说的全对。有审美部分但也有系统思考部分 like 这怎么 fit 系统？有我们在哪、这是什么 theme 一部分？有怎么 present 这个。(00:11:35)：很多是更广 context。显然有些品味部分 like 嘿这个 interaction animation 不 fit 它该有的语义含义。对它试图传达的太 snappy。那 incredibly 重要我可能 focus 太多。(00:11:52)：但有 like 这该是什么？如果我们能 build 任何东西这里 goal 是什么怎么到？我觉得那是 real 品味问题。

turns.en: Yeah. I tend to think that there are some practical reasons why it's lagged and also some harder problems to crack. I'm not in our research org, I'm sure I'll get yelled at for saying us. I think design's a little bit harder to grade than software. And that creating a loop where you can train the model and what's good design and what's bad design is just a little bit more tedious and onerous than does the code compile, does it do what it's supposed to? (00:13:09): Because the human aspect of taste is part of the feedback mechanism you need. I also think that the labs historically invest in making their models good at things that accelerate AI research. And that in the early era of coding models, it was very clear that the model being able to write correct code would accelerate research. In a way that you can't really make the same case for design. Not that getting good at design isn't important, it's that it's not directly in that flywheel. (00:13:46): Those are practical reasons and those will go away. These models will get pretty good at design. There are some kind of murkier things that is going to be really tough. I have kind of a short list of them. One is there is an aspect of culture to what is considered good design. In that you remember it was probably what last year where every new website that came out was just a copy of Linear's website. (00:14:15): Linear's website, great design, great taste. If a model did that, I'd be like, "Wow, this is incredible leaps here." If I have a model that outputs Linear's website every time, that's not the challenge here. There's an amount of novelty that is more important in design than it actually is in software engineering. Software engineering, you must want it to over-index unknown patterns. Whereas design, it's like, "No, there's an element of randomness here and novelty." (00:14:48): To me, I spent a lot of time writing code or supervising code on the early Codex app. And even as the models get good at design, there's sort of an abstraction layer that is an interplay between the software design and the code that's being written. This thing over here in this corner should share X, Y, and Z in the code base with this thing down here. (00:15:14): And that's a little bit different than saying the model needs to be a better designer. Especially that is visual design, but it is significantly deeper. It's about the abstractions in that like, "Oh, if tomorrow our company did a rebrand, the shallow version of this is that we have to update 263 components one by one." The deep version is the semantics between these two things that look different. They're both in list that have this style, that convey this interaction pattern to the user. (00:15:48): And I think that is still feeling a little bit out of reach with the current technology, that abstraction layer. So I think as we've gone through this process of, we started the Codex app in November. And we weren't using it full-time, now we use it for everything. That's been a journey. But now it's like the things that we actually do while using it are different things. So what was the question?
turns.zh: 对。我倾向有些实际原因它 lag 也有更难问题。我不在我们研究 org、肯定会被骂我说 us。我觉得设计比软件更难评分。建 loop 训模型什么好设计什么坏设计比代码编译吗、做该做的更 tedious 和 onerous。(00:13:09)：因为人品味方面是你需要的反馈机制。我也觉得 lab 历史上 invest 让模型擅长加速 AI 研究的事。在早期编程模型时代很清楚模型能写对代码会加速研究。你没法对设计 make 同样 case。不是擅长设计不重要是它不直接在那个 flywheel。(00:13:46)：那些是实际原因会消失。这些模型会变 pretty 擅长设计。有些更 murky 的东西会很难。我有个短 list。一是好设计有文化方面。你记得大概去年每个新网站出来都是 Linear 网站副本。(00:14:15)：Linear 网站好设计好品味。如果模型做那个我会 like 哇这里 incredible 跨越。如果我有个模型每次输出 Linear 网站那不是这里挑战。设计里 novelty 量比软件工程里更重要。软件工程你要它 over-index 已知 pattern。设计是 like 不这里有 random 和 novelty 元素。(00:14:48)：对我来说我花很多时间写代码或 supervise 早期 Codex app 代码。即使模型变擅长设计那里……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know, that was an amazing answer. Speaking of design and being creative, the Codex app when it came out, it's like such a new thing that nobody had seen before. It's not a terminal thing, it's not an ID thing. It's like this chat thing that codes and you could see code. (00:16:32): To your point, it feels like it'd be hard for AI to be like, "Here's a whole new paradigm for how to code." And that feels like where human brains continue to be valuable for now is creativity almost in coming up with something new versus patterns of things that have been done before.
turns.zh: 我知道那是 amazing 回答。说到设计和创意，Codex app 出来时是那么新没人见过。不是终端东西、不是 IDE 东西。是这个 chat 东西编程你能看代码。(00:16:32)：如你所说感觉 AI 很难 like 这是全新编程范式。感觉人脑继续 valuable 的是创意、想出新东西 vs 之前做过的 pattern。

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I totally hear you. Let's give it up for the human brain.
turns.zh: 对。完全听到你。为人类大脑鼓掌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For now. As we were getting ready for this, you said that you were listening to the episode with Jenny who does the head of design for Claude Code and Cowork and such. And she had this whole kind of thesis that the design process is dead. (00:17:02): There's no time for design. Things are moving too fast. Just build now and design is kind of steering things as things move along. You're implying you have kind of a different perspective on the design process.
turns.zh: 暂时。我们准备时你说你在听 Jenny 那期——Claude Code 和 Cowork 等的设计负责人。她有这个 thesis 设计过程死了。(00:17:02)：没时间设计。东西 move 太快。就 build 现在、设计在东西 along 时 steering。你暗示你对设计过程有不同 perspective。

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: We probably agree on a lot of this, Jenny and I. I wasn't a fan of the design. The design process proper, I agree with her take that it is dead. I genuinely was not a fan of this process before AI.
turns.zh: 我和 Jenny 可能很多同意。我不是 design fan。设计过程 proper 我同意她 take 它死了。我 genuinely 在 AI 之前就不 fan 这个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you describe the process real quick just from people think about the design? What does that mean?
turns.zh: 能快速描述过程给想设计的人？那是什么意思？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah. So I mean, when I ran a startup a number of years ago, we would do design hiring. And there was this sort of snarky article that came out about the case study factory. And it was like mid-SERP era stuff and it was that designers were being taught about this process and valuing that above all else, above all outcomes even. (00:17:55): And if something went through this process that two things were true. One, it would be good and the process would guarantee quality and guarantee impact. And also that if something, the thing was good if it went through that process, even if you don't like it and nobody uses it. (00:18:13): And it's like the process of user research and the divergence and the convergence, it's the right framework. It was always a little academic. But I think this is really exposing some areas where it falls down, especially because of the speed of implementation. (00:18:31): And once again, that process is sort of predicated on the assumption that implementation is expensive and that you can really only afford to build once. And so you need to fully, exhaustively go through the problem space and the solution space before implementing. (00:18:51): And then we saw with Figma and Origami and all of these tools that you can fast-forward some of the insights by pulling interactive prototypes earlier into the process. That you can simulate production. And there ended up being sort of a meme about executives just being like, "Well, can we just do a prototype and then expect it to work?" (00:19:15): But this thing was real that this became part of the design process proper. We pulled prototyping into that. The problem now is that you can pull all of the implementation into that and there's a mismatch between, I think a lot of assumptions. (00:19:31): Again, you see this fully polished prototype that looks like it's ready to go out the door. And enough people at a company see that and they're like, "Can we release this now?" But the appropriate, we're actually in that early design process stage and nobody's just saying that. This is where we are with a bunch of multiplayer exploration. (00:19:52): 90 people will have this idea. It'll look really polished, but it's like, "No, this is actually..." That's the design process now. Tying the design process to mediums, media, that's the scary part. It's that designers have more tools now to do this process with. (00:20:12): You can put stuff into the current product and you can A/B test it or just use that as a prototype. Many companies right now have this idea of a baby version of the product. Like baby Cursor, you've seen this on Twitter. We have baby Codex, a dramatically simplified code base that approximates all of the interactions of the production app. And therefore is a lot quicker to vibe code over. Because you can be like, "Well, what if the sidebar worked like this? Or what if a pane came in and had a group chat here? What if X, Y, Z?" That's a huge tool that's part of the design process. (00:20:46): So to say that the design process is dead, I feel like it's both true and false. It's that if you are tied to the tools and the exact day-to-day specifics of the process, then yeah, it's dead. You're not going to have a good time. But to throw the process out completely or throw the overlay of the process, the like, "Hey, we are at this point in the process." That is still more important than ever.
turns.zh: 对。我几年前 run 创业公司时做设计 hiring。有篇 snarky 文章出来关于 case study factory。mid-SERP 时代东西、设计师被教这个过程、valuing 那个 above 一切 even above outcome。(00:17:55)：如果东西经过这个流程两件事 true。一它会好、过程保证质量和影响。也如果东西经过那个流程它是好的即使你不喜欢、没人用。(00:18:13)：就像 user research 和 divergence 和 convergence 的过程。对的 framework。总有点 academic。但我觉得这真暴露一些它 fall down 的地方尤其因为实现速度。(00:18:31)：再说那个过程 sort of predicated on 假设实现贵、你真只能 afford build 一次。所以你需要完全、exhaustively 过问题空间和解决空间 before 实现。(00:18:51)：然后我们看到 Figma 和 Origami 这些工具你能 fast-forward 一些 insight 通过拉 interactive prototype 更早进过程。你能模拟生产。然后有 meme 关于高管就 well 能就做 prototype 然后期望它 work 吗？(00:19:15)：但这个是真的、这变成设计过程 proper 一部分。我们把 prototyping 拉进那个。现在问题是你能拉所有实现进那个、有很多 assumption 之间 mismatch。(00:19:31)：再次你看到这个 fully polished prototype 看起来 ready 出门。公司够多人看到就我们能 release 吗？但合适的我们 actual……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's really interesting because you have a background in every function. If people look at your LinkedIn, it's like engineer, designer, product manager, founder. Now you oversee the desktop app. And I think design is not under your purview, is that right? Is there a separate design team or are they under your?
turns.zh: 有趣因为你背景跨每个职能。如果人看你 LinkedIn 就工程师、设计师、PM、创始人。现在你管桌面 app。设计不在你管下对吧？有独立设计团队还是在你下？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Depends on the week.
turns.zh: 取决于周。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: We worked very closely together. We believe in, while sitting together, being embedded. Reporting line, I don't know.
turns.zh: 我们非常紧密 work。我们相信坐一起、嵌入。Reporting line 我不知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They shift weekly. What does the design process look like on the Codex app?
turns.zh: 它们每周 shift。Codex app 上设计过程长什么样？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah, there's been a lot written about role collapse, existential role collapse. There are no roles anymore. We haven't seen that. We have seen more role collapse in the Codex org than I think other parts of the company and other parts of the economy. I think part of this is that this was a technical product for engineers. And so our designers speak engineer, our product managers speak technical language and write code. (00:22:08): Alexander has a master's degree in computer science, which is, I do not have a master's degree in computer science. So we've seen a lot of role collapse. And I think that one of the ways that we describe how the groups work together is that there's significantly more overlap in the roles than there used to be. And everybody's sort of defined less by the fence and the boundaries of where design stops and engineering starts, but more the average of where they're working. (00:22:37): So if you average up all of the things that somebody on our design team does, there's plenty of code writing things. There's plenty of things that are product work, but on average there are dots over here if you draw it out on a diagram. And this sort of speaks to the process too, especially because the entirety of the Codex app has been informed by the dog fooding loop. (00:23:02): There is a desire among all of us to try to do as much as possible in the app even when it's not the best tool, so that it can become the best tool. And so a lot of design we all work on by using the app and say, "Okay, what's broken about this?" This is a whole thing we do, which is that we often don't improve our process so that we can make the product better to do it, which is a deeply uncomfortable place to be in. But week to week, it's changing.
turns.zh: 对，关于角色 collapse、existential 角色 collapse 写了很多。没有角色了。我们没看到那个。我们在 Codex org 看到比公司其他部分和经济其他部分更多角色 collapse。我觉得部分这是给工程师的技术产品。所以我们的设计师说工程师语言、我们的 PM 说技术语言、写代码。(00:22:08)：Alexander 有计算机科学硕士学位，我没有。所以我们看到很多角色 collapse。我觉得我们描述 group 怎么一起 work 的方式之一是角色间显著更多 overlap。每个人 less defined by 设计停哪工程开始的 fence 和 boundary，更多他们 work 哪里的 average。(00:22:37)：所以如果你 average 起我们设计团队某人做的一切有大量写代码的事。有大量产品工作但平均他们点在这边如果你画图。这也 speak to 过程尤其因为整个 Codex app 由 dogfooding loop inform。(00:23:02)：我们所有人渴望试在 app 里做尽可能多即使它不是最好工具这样它能成最好工具。所以设计我们大家都用 app work 说好这什么坏了？这是我们做的 whole thing，我们常不改进我们过程这样能让产品更好做它，这是 deeply uncomfortable place。但每周在变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this point so much that what are you? It's your role is the average of what you spend your time on. If most of your work is PM-y work, then okay, you're PM for now. If it's engineering, you're an engineer for now. I feel like, was OpenAI the first company to call people member of technical staff?
turns.zh: 我爱这个点 so much 就是说你是什么？你的角色是你花时间的 average。如果大多工作 PM-y 那好你暂时 PM。如果是工程你暂时工程师。感觉 OpenAI 是第一个叫人 member of technical staff 的公司吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: No, I believe that this might've started with Xerox. First company I interned at, it was a company called Upthere, did the same thing. This has been around. But it's much more common now, but it is kind of a tradition in research focused companies, right?
turns.zh: 不，我相信这可能从 Xerox 开始。我实习的第一家公司叫 Upthere 做一样。这存在很久。但现在更普遍，是研究聚焦公司的传统对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, got it. So it emerged from research. But I feel like it's such a, I don't know, sign of where things might be headed, this idea of we're just going to call everyone member of technical staff, your function isn't set. You're not in this bucket of the PM org or the eng org or the design org. (00:24:16): Do you feel like that's where we all head long-term? Do you feel like functions will continue to exist? There's still the PM skillset and the eng skillset and the design skillset. And people are, "I'm a designer." Or do you think this is like, people call it builder. Do you feel like there's this collapse coming where everyone's everything and that's just the future? Or do you think we're going to continue to be mostly divided up in quadrants?
turns.zh: 好懂。所以从研究出来。但我觉得这是那么……不知道……事情往哪走的 sign，这个我们叫所有人 member of technical staff、你的 function 不固定。你不在 PM org 或 eng org 或 design org 桶。(00:24:16)：你觉得那是我们长期都往哪走？你觉得 function 会继续存在？仍有 PM skillset 和 eng skillset 和 design skillset。人是我是设计师。或你觉得这是大家叫 builder。你觉得有 collapse 在来大家什么都做、那就是未来？还是你觉得继续大多分 quadrant？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah. There are some things that I'm afraid of. And I think that some companies like to be very extreme about getting onto the bandwagon of whatever people say is going to happen. And I think part of the danger in eliminating the concept of roles is that it can dangerously eliminate the idea that things are specialties with knowable best practices. (00:25:10): I've heard a lot of companies be like, "We're getting rid of the product role," which I think is by the way, a terrible idea. And everybody's just going to be a builder. And then what happens is this whole discipline of product that's been built up and has real best practices, real things that have been tried and failed, and real processes, that just gets abandoned. Because people are like, "Oh, I wrote some code." That's not a great place to be in. (00:25:37): I think that the boundary of so and-so, this isn't your lane. I welcome that part going away. But there's a balance here where it's like not everyone can work on everything, for one, both in terms of breadth and depth rate. This is why managers are not going to go away. (00:25:58): Not everybody can work on everything. And also every discipline has a skill component to it, which I think a lot of engineers are guilty of not recognizing that, "Well, engineering has a skill to it. It's writing code and other roles are just people vibing." It's like, "No, that's not how it works." Yes, you can use Excel, but you cannot work on the finance team, that kind of stuff, right?
turns.zh: 对。有些我害怕的。我觉得一些公司喜欢很极端 jump 上大家说会发生的 bandwagon。我觉得去掉角色概念的危险是它能危险地去掉东西是有 knowable best practice 的 specialty 这个 idea。(00:25:10)：我听到很多公司 like 我们去掉产品角色——我觉得顺便 terrible idea——每个人都 builder。然后发生的是产品这整个 discipline 建起来、有真 best practice、真试过失败的事、真流程，那个就 abandoned。因为人 like 哦我写了代码。那不是 great place。(00:25:37)：我觉得某某这不是你 lane 的 boundary 我欢迎那部分走。但有 balance 这里 like 不是人人能 work on 一切，一 breadth 二 depth rate。这是为什么 manager 不会走。(00:25:58)：不是人人能 work on 一切。也每个 discipline 有 skill 组件我觉得很多工程师 guilty 不认识到嗯工程有 skill 是写代码、其他角色就是人 vibing。就像不不是那样 work。对你能用 Excel 但你不能在财务团队 work 那种对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think there's also just like, "Do you want to be doing this work?"
turns.zh: 对。我觉得也就像你想做这个 work 吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do I want to be?
turns.zh: 我想吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: I think more of it's that actually now, is it's easier to switch roles. It's easier to learn the best practices. It's easier to not tie your effectiveness in a role with the ability to use the exact tool. It's more of like, "Can you get yourself into this mindset, learn which things work and which don't, and then focus on it?" (00:26:52): I spent so long feeling like I should not be a software engineer because I didn't care about assembly language or memorizing type scripts and texts. And it's like there have always been parts to these roles that are that sort of gatekeeping. That are like, "Well, no, being good at this role is being good at this tool." And I think that's what's kind of starting to erode. I think people take this, they hyperbolize all of this.
turns.zh: 我觉得更多其实是现在、更容易 switch 角色。更容易学 best practice。更容易不 tie 你在角色的 effectiveness 和用确切工具的能力。更多像你能让自己进这个 mindset、学哪些 work 哪些不、然后 focus？(00:26:52)：我那么久觉得我不该是软件工程师因为我不在乎汇编语言或记 typescript 和 text。这些角色总有那种 gatekeeping 部分。像 well 不擅长这个角色是擅长这个工具。我觉得那是开始 erode 的。我觉得大家 take 这个、hyperbolize 这一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does your team look like on the Codex team? How many engineers, designers, PMs? What's kind of the makeup of the team right now?
turns.zh: 你 Codex 团队团队长什么样？多少工程师、设计师、PM？团队现在 makeup 大致？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Every time people ask me how many people are on the Codex team, do you remember my answer to this? I'm like, "It's somewhere between 10 and a few thousand." I mean, it's like a fake answer, but it's real in that we do see this as the culmination of what everybody works on here. (00:27:45): Everything that goes into model research, everything that goes into how models are good at CUA and browser use. Everything about how model personality. All of the product work around front end infrastructure, all of the user, all of it is this product. At the same time, we are not accepting PRs daily from thousands and thousands of people on whatever they want. (00:28:07): So we got a team, double digits of engineers, probably half that on the design side. A few product people, although product here is kind of more of a zone defense play. And I think one thing that is very common among everybody on the Codex side or on the desktop side is agency and taste, right? (00:28:29): A lot of former founders or people who were at larger companies doing founder shaped things. A lot of people with immense taste. At OpenAI, we let teams get very large. So we haven't said, "Hey, there's no management," but the teams are quite large. It's mostly ICs and I think that's good.
turns.zh: 每次人问我 Codex 团队多少人你记得我回答？我就 between 10 和几千。fake 回答但 real 因为我们确实看这是大家在这 work 的一切 culmination。(00:27:45)：一切进模型 research、一切进模型怎么擅长 CUA 和浏览器使用。一切关于模型人格。所有前端基础设施产品工作、所有 user、所有都是这个产品。同时我们不接受每天几千人 PR 随便什么。(00:28:07)：所以我们有团队、双位数工程师、大概一半设计。几个产品人虽然这里产品更多 zone defense play。我觉得 Codex 侧或桌面侧每个人很 common 的是 agency 和品味对吧？(00:28:29)：很多前创始人或在更大公司做 founder shaped 事的人。很多 immense 品味的人。OpenAI 我们让团队变得很大。所以我们没说嘿没管理但团队挺大。大多 IC 我觉得 good。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You use this term zone defense for product work and that's really interesting. It kind of maps to the design kind of shift also, just like you're there to manage and coordinate. Talk a little bit more about what that looks like. What does zone defense look like for a product person?
turns.zh: 你用 zone defense 这个术语 for 产品工作那很有趣。它 map 到设计 shift 也、就像你在那管理和协调。多聊聊那个长什么样。产品人 zone defense 长什么样？

turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: Yeah. And I have had a lot of conversations with Alexander about this analogy, which is that if two product people are working too closely, that's often not a good signal. And that you kind of want, as a product org, you sort of want to do this force directed activity. Where you're like, "Where are the gaps?" (00:29:22): Especially in this new world where curation and steering and alignment is a lot of things. Where you're like, "There's a ton of chaos happening on people throwing ideas all over the place." The whole top down, year long planning thing, not going to work. (00:29:36): And so now it's like we need the taste makers to guide things from inception to what the product should be. And that means you basically want company coverage. And so you spread out and you say, "All right, who's best at what? Let's create some space between us so that we got full coverage." And that's kind of how it goes. (00:29:55): And then you fill in the gaps and you're like, "Look, we want to hire engineers who are product-minded." We don't want it to be that we've got a bunch of people writing a bunch of code that needs full team reviewing it for product coherence. (00:42:39): And we did that super quick dog fooding loop because you've got your personal dog fooding loop. Where you're like, "Oh, I can't do this thing. (00:43:41): There was a release or a series of releases in May-ish that introduced the in-app browser, computer use, and artifact creation to the Codex app. That was, I think our Codex is for almost everyone release. turns.speaker: Andrew Ambrosino
turns.en: We had Codex as a CLI and then we decided to build this app. And we were a little uncertain about the app but had a lot of conviction in what it could be as to start a developer tool. (00:52:35): And it wasn't going to be an ITE, it was going to be this right sized surface. Where it was sort of a chatbot but it was more than that and you could see the code but we weren't going to let you edit the code. (00:52:45): There's a really interesting thing that happened at OpenAI in January and February. And it was before we actually released the Codex app, which is that we'd started to dog food the Codex app. And what we were finding, we were converging on some pretty clear internal PMF on engineering and research workflows. (00:53:08): They were thrilled. They were loving it. We were like, "All right, we just got to get the quality bar up before we release it to the world. We're convinced that this will be a thing." But then at the company, we spun up a few other workflows to say, "Hey, this Codex effort is onto something with these coding agents." (00:53:23): And we have people from marketing, from comms, from finance, from legal, from basically every discipline, who are using this Codex app, even though it is actively hostile to these people. It is trying to show them code. It's trying to ask for approval to run RG on the... (00:53:41): It's doing all of these things that are actively not the right product surface for them. So why don't we take our other surfaces and add Codex to them? Let's add it to the ChatGPT desktop app. Let's add it to the Atlas browser. And let's essentially take the lessons of Codex and make it more general for a general knowledge work tool. (00:54:02): And those efforts went for a little bit. And the most annoying problem happened, which is nobody would leave the Codex app for the apps that were allegedly for these other personas. I think the lesson in all of this was just that the whole developer tool versus general knowledge work tool, there's a lot of nuance here that isn't just one or the other. (00:54:25): I think we believe really strongly in this. And that there are certainly, in the same way that we talk about the average of your role as what your role is now, this is true on the product side too. (00:54:36): People who are doing Excel work don't want to see Git repository information. We know that, but we also know that we can tell a lot from what they're doing about what kind of work they do. And we can start simple, grow the product to complex as we feel is needed. (00:54:53): It doesn't mean we don't have modes. You might want some modes for organizing your stuff and to sort of be legible about the ways that you enter the experience. But we really believe strongly that what we've built here is the right shape to take on really deep, vertically focused things. (00:55:13): We work deeply with our finance team, with our team working on science, team working on legal. And we say, "If we can build the right extensibility primitives in the right general model, then you can do anything with this." And then our challenge is, well, how do you generalize it? (00:55:33): But this is kind of going back to the best desktop app that we can build. What does that look like? And so it was Codex the developer tool, ChatGPT, where's this going? This is how we think about it.
